topics.title: Start
topics.teach: This lesson is Interviews for internships, scholarships, and work. You will draft answers from your own experience and check one answer the way the interview rubric does. A partner, a printed packet, and a Google account are not required. The pre-check asks what you think before the teaching. The official questions stay on the assessment, not on this page. The lesson practices hoʻokūpono.

fields.label: I am ready for the pre-check

topics.title: First impression
topics.teach: Landing an interview is the first step. How you answer can decide a scholarship, a college offer, or a job. During an interview, keep eye contact, answer the whole question, use an example that fits the question, ask for clarification when you need it, and speak clearly and slowly enough for the interviewer to follow. Wear clothing that fits the workplace you are interviewing for. An employer cannot ask about your health, or whether you have a disability, unless the job states a health requirement. You decide whether to disclose a disability.

items.label: Ask if you need the question repeated
Employer asks about a disability when the job lists no health requirement
Use an example that fits the question

fields.name: clothes
fields.label: Name a role, then one thing you would wear for that workplace

topics.title: Questions
topics.teach: Common interview questions are not worded the same way every time, but the intention is the same. Prepare several of them. The list includes: tell me about yourself; how you heard about the position; who else you are interviewing with; how other people would describe you; a professional or academic achievement; what you know about the organization; why you want the position; why they should accept you; your strengths; your weaknesses; a challenge and how you dealt with it; where you see yourself in five years; your dream job; what you want in a position; the work environment you prefer; a time you led; a time you disagreed; how you handle pressure; what you do outside of work; an animal you would be; and whether you have questions for them. A useful way to predict questions is to read the qualifications and the duties of the role.

fields.label: One question you will prepare
options: Tell me a little about yourself.
What do you consider to be your weaknesses?
Tell me about a challenge you faced and how you dealt with it.
Where do you see yourself in five years?
Why do you want this position?

topics.title: STAR
topics.teach: For a challenge question, use STAR. Situation is the context. Task is what you were supposed to do. Action is what you did. Result is what changed. Worked example: Situation, in English class the group worked in small groups. Task, each person had an assigned role. Action, nobody liked the roles, so one student suggested they each do what they were best at. Result, the group worked together better than before. Write a different challenge from your own school, work, or family life. Do not copy that example.

topics.title: Draft
topics.teach: Use the resume from the college application lesson if you have it. If you do not, use a skill you have actually practiced. About yourself: give two or three facts, then two or three accomplishments, and say why you fit. A strength should be specific and related to the role. Excellent communication is more specific than people person. A weakness should include what you are already doing to get better. Disclosing a disability here is your choice.

topics.title: Practice
topics.teach: If someone is with you, they ask one question and score your pace, clarity, and example. They also notice body language, including whether you sit up or look uninterested. If you are alone, use the empty chair: say the answer out loud, score yourself on the same speaking scale, note your posture, then say it once more and fix the weak part.

topics.title: Feedback
topics.teach: After a practice interview, compare what went well with what you would change. You can also ask a real interviewer for one suggestion to use next time. That shows you want to learn. Write the improvement you would make, and one question you would ask them about the role. Do not share someone else's personal story.

fields.label: One thing you will do differently next time

fields.label: One question you would ask the interviewer

topics.title: Wrap
topics.teach: Interview practice raises the chance of being hired, admitted, or awarded a scholarship. You can teach the same questions at home so other people can practice. Your own background can be useful when the organization serves your community. Reading the organization's goals helps you name a skill they need. It is okay to apply for a role you are not fully qualified for. The interview is still practice, and you can show the skills you do have and how you would learn the rest.
